title: Mapwork: the skills of the extract

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Everything a map extract asks: grid references, directions and bearings, distances, heights and cross-sections, the key, and reading the landscape from the evidence, relief, drainage, settlement, communications and land use.

blocks.heading: Grid references
blocks.text: A map is divided into squares by eastings, the vertical lines numbered west to east, and northings, the horizontal lines numbered south to north. A four-figure reference names a whole square by the lines at its bottom-left corner: square 4664 is the square whose corner is easting 46 and northing 64. A six-figure reference locates a point inside the square by adding a third figure to each pair: the tenths of the way across, then the tenths of the way up. The order is fixed, eastings first, then northings, along the corridor, then up the stairs, and the figures come from the grid lines, never from road numbers or other labels on the sheet. A point halfway across square 4664 and three-tenths up is 465463: the easting 46 becomes 465, the northing 64 becomes 643.

blocks.heading: Directions and bearings
blocks.text: A compass direction is a point of the compass, given as the direction of one place from another: north-north-east, south-west, east. A bearing is different: an angle measured clockwise from grid north, in degrees, so east is 090, south is 180 and west is 270. A bearing of 135 is south-east; the two answers name the same direction in different systems, and a question asks for one or the other by name. Bearings are measured clockwise from grid north with a protractor, its centre on the starting point and its zero line along grid north.

blocks.heading: Distances along a route
blocks.text: To measure a straight-line distance, lay the paper's edge between the two points, mark both, and set the marks against the scale line. To measure a distance along a route, a road, a river, a path, follow the route with the straight edge of a sheet of paper, marking each bend on the paper as you go, then lay the whole chain of marks on the scale line and read the total. A straight-line measurement between the ends underestimates a winding route, sometimes badly. On a 1:50 000 map, 1 centimetre on the map is 0.5 kilometres on the ground; on a 1:25 000 map, 1 centimetre is 0.25 kilometres. A route measuring 6.4 centimetres on the 1:50 000 sheet is 6.4 x 0.5 = 3.2 kilometres on the ground.

blocks.heading: Heights from contours
blocks.text: Contours join points of equal height, shown on most extracts every 10 metres. Read them in three ways. The height of a place is the contour it sits on or between, or the spot height printed at the point, which is exact where the contour is approximate. The difference in height between two places is the highest contour crossed minus the lowest: from the 40-metre contour to the 120-metre contour is 120 - 40 = 80 metres of climb. The spacing of the contours gives the steepness: bunched contours mean a steep slope, widely spaced ones a gentle one, and a cluster of contours close together against a contour far apart marks a cliff. A triangulation pillar marks a surveyed high point.

blocks.heading: Cross-sections
blocks.text: A cross-section shows the shape of the land along a line drawn on the map. Draw the line, mark every contour it crosses, and plot each crossing against distance and height on a grid: the line joining the plotted points is the profile of the slope. The vertical scale is usually drawn larger than the horizontal scale to make the shape readable, which is vertical exaggeration, and the exaggeration should be stated so the reader knows the slopes look steeper than they are. A section that rises in steps is a gentle slope becoming a steep one; a section with a broad low flat stretch between two rises is a valley with a flood plain in the middle.

blocks.heading: Translating the scale
blocks.text: A feature's real size is its map measurement multiplied by the scale. On a 1:50 000 map, a wood measuring 3 centimetres across is 3 x 0.5 = 1.5 kilometres wide on the ground; a 4-centimetre stretch of coast on a 1:25 000 sheet is 4 x 0.25 = 1 kilometre. The same conversion turns a real distance into a map distance for planning: 2 kilometres on the ground is 2 / 0.5 = 4 centimetres on the 1:50 000 sheet. Describing a feature in real terms, the width of the estuary, the length of the ridge, is this multiplication, and the answer carries its unit, kilometres.

blocks.heading: The key
blocks.text: The key is read before the map, because the symbols are the map's vocabulary. Each symbol carries a precise category: the key says national road, not highway; coniferous plantation, not trees; nonconiferous woodland, not wood. An answer that names a feature with the key's own term is right, and a general term is not. The symbols carry more than names: the width of a road symbol shows the road's importance, the style of a building symbol shows its use, a school, a church, a hospital, and the colour of an area shows its cover, blue for water, green for woodland, white for open ground.

blocks.heading: Drawing inferences from the map
blocks.text: A map is evidence, and the skill is to draw what it supports. Settlements cluster where the land is flat and water is near, so a line of villages along a valley floor is no accident; roads avoid the steepest gradients, so a main road that bends round a spur is taking the gentle way; land use follows the relief, so the rough grazing sits on the steep slopes and the arable fields on the flat. Every inference is drawn from stated evidence, the feature read from the map, the pattern it makes, and the conclusion the pattern supports, and an inference that names no evidence is a guess.

blocks.heading: Describing landscape features
blocks.text: A landscape description names the features and their character with geographical terms and simple adjectives: a wide flat-floored valley, a steep convex slope, a rocky headland, a nucleated village on the valley floor. The terms are the syllabus's own, the adjectives are simple, and together they say what the landscape is like without explaining it. Relief is the height and shape of the land; drainage is the water on it, the rivers and streams, their pattern, density and flow direction; the two are described separately, and a drainage feature that is not on the map cannot be described from it.

blocks.heading: Drainage and the relief
blocks.text: Drainage density is the length of stream channels per unit area. A wet upland carries closely spaced streams between bunched contours, high density; a dry lowland carries a few streams in wide valleys, low density. Stream patterns read from the shape of their joining: a dendritic pattern, branches like a tree, suits uniform rock; streams bending round parallel spurs mark a valley side; a stream flowing between two spurs sits in the syncline the contours draw. The flow direction comes from the heights: water flows from the high ground to the low, so the contours at the stream's two ends settle which way it runs.

blocks.heading: Coastlines and river channels
blocks.text: On a large-scale map a coastline reads three ways: cliffs show as a hard edge with contours bunched against it, a beach as a flat strip at sea level beside the low-water mark, and a marsh as flat ground with the wet symbols, reeds or tidal marks. A river channel changes downstream: a narrow, straight channel in the upper square, meanders and a broader channel in the middle, and a wide mouth with marsh in the last, because the discharge grows as tributaries join.

blocks.heading: Land use
blocks.text: Land use follows the land. Improved pasture and arable fields sit on the flat lowland where the ground can be ploughed; rough grazing climbs the slopes that machinery cannot; woodland clothes the steepest ground, where nothing else pays; settlement strings along the main routes. The map shows the pattern, the field shapes large and rectangular on the planned lowland, small and irregular on the old common land, and the inference comes from matching the use to the relief that suits it.

blocks.heading: Settlement patterns
blocks.text: Settlements sit in three patterns. Nucleated: the buildings grouped round a centre, a church, a green, a junction, the old defensive and market shape. Linear: the buildings strung along a line, a road or a valley floor, each house taking its frontage from the route. Dispersed: farms scattered across the area with no centre, the pattern of enclosure country where each holding stands on its own land. The pattern is described from the map, and its reason inferred: nucleation suits a village with a church and services, linear suits a route through enclosed ground, dispersal suits large farms worked from the homestead.

blocks.heading: Urban morphology
blocks.text: A town's shape reads on the large-scale sheet in zones. At the centre, a dense grid of tightly packed blocks, the commercial heart, with the market square, the chain stores and the offices. Around it, terraced streets and semi-detached rows, the nineteenth-century growth, small regular plots along straight streets. At the edge, detached housing with gardens and the post-war estates, where the streets curve and the plots widen, and beyond them the retail park and the bypass, the newest growth with its car parks. Reading the zones is reading the town's history, and the pattern of one zone into the next is the urban morphology the map shows.

blocks.heading: Functions, services, site and growth
blocks.text: A settlement's function is what it does, its main economic and social activities: a port town with docks and warehouses, a market town with a livestock market and a coaching inn, a resort with a promenade and a golf course. Its services are what it provides, the school, the hospital, the college, and the two together tell the region what the settlement is for. The site, the land the town stands on, was chosen for what it offered: dry flat ground, a water supply, a bridging point, a sheltered harbour or a defensive spur. Growth then followed the routes and the work: the town on the bridging point grew where the roads converged on its bridge.

blocks.heading: Communication networks
blocks.text: Communications are read in type and density. Type: motorway, dual carriageway, main road, minor road, track, mainline railway, branch line, navigable river, each with its own symbol and its own speed. Density: how close the routes stand, thick on the lowland where the settlement is dense, thin in the upland where each valley carries one road. The network follows the land, because routes take the cheapest gradient: the motorway runs along the flat, the minor road threads the valley, and the paths cross the ridge at the saddle where the climb is least.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: Every theme of Papers 1 and 4 arrives on Paper 2 as a resource: population as pyramids and densities, rivers as channel shapes and drainage patterns, settlements as morphology and function, development as data to plot. The skills here are the toolkit, and the four map extracts used in the cards are the practice ground.

blocks.heading: Grid references, worked
blocks.text:
A worked extract to practise on; each cell is one grid square, with north at the top.

| northing \\ easting | 62 | 63 | 64 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 65 | ford, stream | village of Okapuka, church | plantation, track |
| 64 | steep slope, contours 40-80 m | main road junction | saw mill |
| 63 | marsh, reeds | farmstead, borehole | quarry |
The ford sits in the square at easting 62, northing 65, so its four-figure reference is 6265. The church stands in the middle of square 6365, which is five-tenths across and five-tenths up, so its six-figure reference is 635655: the easting 63 gains its fifth to make 635, the northing 65 gains its fifth to make 655, and the easting is written first, along the corridor before up the stairs. A learner who writes 655635 has the two halves in the wrong order and points somewhere near the marsh instead. Paper 2 sets these skills on a large-scale map extract with a printed key, or on a graph, table, photograph or diagram, and each part is usually worth one to three marks.

blocks.heading: Grid references: the common error
blocks.text: The error the registers record is northings written before eastings, or a figure lifted from a road number. The correct move is the fixed order: eastings from the top or bottom of the grid first, then northings from the side, and the third figures estimated inside the square, never borrowed from a label on the map. The test that tells them apart: along before up, and the figures come from the grid lines alone.

blocks.heading: Direction and bearing, worked
blocks.text: On the worked extract above, the farmstead sits in square 6363 and the quarry in 6463, one square to the east, so the quarry's direction from the farmstead is due east. The saw mill, in square 6464, is one square east and one square north of the farmstead, so its direction is north-east, and its bearing, measured clockwise from grid north, is 045 degrees. A learner who gives 45 degrees as a compass direction has confused the two systems: a direction is a point of the compass such as north-east, a bearing is degrees clockwise from grid north, and a question asks for one by name. Paper 2 usually gives one mark for each, and both are read from the grid, not estimated from the drawing.

blocks.heading: Distance, worked
blocks.text: The paper-edge method, worked. A track runs from the farmstead in square 6363 to the saw mill in 6464, bending twice. Lay the straight edge of a sheet of paper along the first straight stretch and mark the bend on the paper; turn the paper at the bend, mark the next; mark the end. The chain of marks now holds the whole route as one straight line. Lay it against the scale line of a 1:50 000 extract, where 1 centimetre is 0.5 kilometres, and read: the marks span 4.4 centimetres, so the track is 4.4 x 0.5 = 2.2 kilometres on the ground. A learner who rules one straight line from farmstead to mill measures 3.6 centimetres and answers 1.8 kilometres, which is the crow's flight and not the track.

blocks.heading: Heights, worked
blocks.text: Contours, worked on a line of them. A footpath leaves the 40-metre contour, crosses the 60, the 80 and the 100, and ends at a spot height of 112 metres. The height gained is 112 - 40 = 72 metres. The spacing tells the steepness: the 40 and 60 contours stand a centimetre apart, the 80 and 100 a finger's width, and where the path meets the 100-metre line the next contours crowd together, so the lower slope is gentle and the upper slope steep. Reading height off a map is this pair: a number from the contours or the spot height, and a gradient from the gaps between them.

blocks.heading: Cross-section, worked
blocks.text: A section line runs from a spot height of 90 metres across a valley to a spot height of 130 metres. Along the way it crosses the 80-metre contour, then the 60 at the stream, then 80 again on the far side. To draw it: rule a horizontal axis for distance and a vertical axis for height, plot each crossing where it occurs, and join the points. The shape that emerges is a valley, a dip to 60 metres at the stream between two shoulders of high ground, and if the vertical axis is drawn larger than the horizontal the slopes look steeper than they are, which is vertical exaggeration, and the honest section states it.

blocks.heading: Scale translation, worked
blocks.text: A reservoir measures 2.8 centimetres long on the 1:50 000 extract: 2.8 x 0.5 = 1.4 kilometres of water. Its dam is 0.3 centimetres thick, which is 0.3 x 0.5 = 0.15 kilometres, about 150 metres, so the drawing's hairline is really a wall 150 metres across. The skill runs both ways: a planner who must show a 3-kilometre stretch of road on the same extract works 3 / 0.5 = 6 centimetres and knows the strip will fill most of the sheet. Describing a feature in real terms is this multiplication said in words, a lake a kilometre and a half long, a dam 150 metres thick.

blocks.heading: The key, worked
blocks.text: A key reads before the map, worked. On the worked extract above the key would carry entries such as ford, marsh with reeds, plantation, quarry, spot height. Asked about the marsh, an answer that calls it a wet place or some water has used a general term; the key's own category is marsh, with the reeds as its symbol. Asked to identify the plantation, the answer names plantation, the key's word, and adds the symbol that proves it, the tree cluster. The habit to build is to match every named feature back to its key entry, because the key's vocabulary is the map's own.

blocks.heading: Inference, worked
blocks.text: Inference from the worked extract, run as evidence then conclusion. Evidence: the village of Okapuka, square 6365, sits on the stream at the ford square, with the main road junction one square south. Inference: the settlement chose the crossing, because a place where a road meets a river needs a ford and a ford gathers travellers, and the village grew where the two routes cross. Each step names what the map shows and what it means, and an inference that skips its evidence reads as a guess, which the resource does not support. Paper 2 asks for this in short parts, a feature, then the pattern, then the conclusion it supports.

blocks.heading: Landscape description, worked
blocks.text: Describing a landscape from the worked extract, in the terms it asks for. The south-west corner: a marsh with reeds on low ground beside the stream, flat and wet. The middle: a village nucleated on its church, a ford on the stream, a road junction serving it. The east: a quarry cut into the rising ground, a saw mill beside the plantation, and the contours climbing from 40 to 80 metres towards the steep slope. The description names each feature with a term and an adjective, marsh, nucleated, steep, and stops at what is shown, which is what a one-mark or two-mark part on Paper 2 rewards.

blocks.heading: Drainage and relief, worked
blocks.text: Drainage worked on the extract above. The stream enters at the ford, square 6265, and flows south-west through the marsh of square 6263, so the flow direction is read from the heights: the ground falls from the 40-to-80-metre steep slope down to the marsh, and water runs downhill. The drainage density is low, one main stream and a marsh on twelve squares, which suits dry country with one valley. Relief is the land, drainage is the water on it, and the two are described separately: the relief climbs from marsh level to 80 metres, the drainage gathers it into one channel.

blocks.heading: Relief is not drainage
blocks.text: The recorded error is describing contours or a road when the drainage is asked for, or naming a channel the map does not show. The correct move: relief is the height and shape of the land surface, drainage is the water on it, its streams, their pattern, density and flow, and both are read from the squares the extract gives. The test: is the answer about the land surface or the water on it, and is the feature actually printed on the extract?

blocks.heading: Coast and channel, worked
blocks.text: A river channel read on a large-scale sheet changes down its course, and the worked table shows it: in the upper squares the channel is narrow and straight between bunched contours; in the middle squares it meanders on a wider flood plain; on the lowest squares it splits into distributaries across a marsh by the sea. Each change is stated with its evidence, narrow and straight, meandering, distributaries, and the reason follows: the discharge grows as tributaries join, so the channel widens and wanders. A coastline reads the same way on the sheet, cliffs as a hard edge with contours against it, a beach as flat ground at the low-water line, and the terms come from the key.

blocks.heading: Land use, worked
blocks.text: Land use worked on the extract above. The marsh square carries reeds, unimproved wet ground. The village square carries settlement. The plantation square carries forestry, and the quarry square carries extraction. The pattern is the ground's own logic: the wet lowland is left as marsh, the dry flat ground holds the village, the steep slope is too poor for fields and wears the plantation, and the quarry sits where the rock outcrops. A Paper 2 part asks for the variation, and the answer gives the uses with their squares and the reason each sits where it does.

blocks.heading: Settlement patterns, worked
blocks.text: The three settlement patterns, worked. Nucleated: the village of Okapuka, its buildings grouped round the church and the ford. Linear: the farmstead strung along the track where it crosses square 6363. Dispersed: the borehole farmstead standing alone in square 6363's neighbours, a single holding on its own land. A sketch map of the patterns is drawn as three boxes, dots clustered, dots in a line, dots scattered, labelled, because the sketch is the fastest way to show a pattern a paragraph would labour. Each pattern is named from the map before it is explained, and the reasons follow, the ford for the village, the route for the line, the holding for the farm.

blocks.heading: Urban morphology, worked
blocks.text: Urban morphology, worked on a town sheet. From the centre outwards: the market square and chain stores in tight blocks; the terraced streets in small regular plots around them; the detached housing with gardens where the plots widen; the retail park and school on the edge by the bypass. The zones are read from the symbols, tight blocks, rows, gardens, car parks, and the order is the town's history, because the middle was built first and each ring followed as travel reached farther. A description on Paper 2 follows that order, and each zone is named with the symbols that mark it.

blocks.heading: Function, services and site, worked
blocks.text: Function and site, worked. A settlement whose symbols are a quay, warehouses and a ferry slipway has the function of a port; one whose symbols are a cathedral, a college and a hospital has the function of a service town; the same grid square can hold both a chapel and a shop, and the larger set of symbols names the dominant function. The site is read the same way: a town on a dry flat spur above a river crossing was sited for defence and the bridge, and its growth followed the routes that converged on the crossing. Function is what it does, services are what it provides, site is the ground it stands on, and the map answers all three by its symbols.

blocks.heading: Communications, worked
blocks.text: Communication networks, worked. On the extract above the main road runs north to south through the junction square, a track links the farmstead to the saw mill, and the footpath crosses the ford. The types are named from the key, sealed main road, track, footpath, and the density is counted: three routes on twelve squares, with the heavy route on the dry ground and the footpath the one route that risks the wet crossing. Relief explains the pattern, because the main road keeps to the gentle ground and the steep slope square carries none. Type, density and the relief behind them are the three things a network answer names.

blocks.heading: A second extract to read end to end
blocks.text:
A second worked extract, read as one connected landscape; each cell is one grid square, north at the top, scale 1:50 000, so 1 centimetre is 0.5 kilometres.

| northing \\ easting | 21 | 22 | 23 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 74 | sea, cliffs 60 m | small bay, sand beach | hotel, promenade |
| 73 | sea | rocky headland, light beacon | golf links |
| 72 | estuary, tidal marsh | harbour, quays | town: offices and chain stores |

The landscape in one paragraph. The west is a hard cliff coast falling 60 metres to the sea, softened once where a small bay holds a sand beach and a hotel behind it. The centre is a headland with a beacon warning shipping off the rocks. The south is an estuary mouth with tidal marsh on its east bank, a harbour with quays, and a town whose offices and chain stores name the place a resort serves. The land use follows the ground, as it does everywhere: the hotel and links on the flat dry ground above the shore, the harbour on the sheltered estuary, the marsh left wet because building there would flood. One extract, and every skill of this unit has something to work on.

blocks.heading: The second extract, skills applied
blocks.text: The same extract, its skills applied one by one. Grid references: the hotel is five-tenths across and five-tenths up square 2374, so its six-figure reference is 235745, eastings first; the beacon, in the middle of 2273, is 225735. Directions and bearings: the harbour at 2272 from the beacon at 2273 is one square south on the same easting, so due south, bearing 180. Distance: the promenade road from the hotel square to the harbour measures 5.2 centimetres along its bends on the paper-edge method, and 5.2 x 0.5 = 2.6 kilometres of coast road. Heights: the cliffs stand 60 metres, and the contour bunching against the shore shows where. Scale translation: the golf links, about 2 centimetres across, cover 2 x 0.5 = 1 kilometre of ground. Each answer names its evidence, the square, the symbol or the measurement, which is the habit the whole unit builds.

blocks.heading: How Paper 2 sets the map
blocks.text: How the paper sets these skills, from the syllabus's own account of Paper 2. The paper tests skills of application, interpretation and analysis of geographical information, on topographical maps, tables of data, other maps, written material, diagrams, photographs and pictorial material and graphs, and the application of graphical and other techniques; candidates answer all the questions, and no place-specific knowledge is needed, because everything the answer needs is on the sheet. The map question typically opens with the key, then a reference, a direction, a distance, a height, and builds to relief, drainage, settlement and land use read as patterns, one to three marks a part, and the total is a third of the paper's marks. Practising the skills on worked extracts like the two above is the whole preparation, because the extract changes and the skills do not.

blocks.heading: Communications read twice, once on each extract
blocks.text: Communications, worked on the coastal extract as well. Its routes are three: the promenade road from the hotel square to the harbour, the coast road the cliff square cannot take, so the road detours inland, and the harbour's quays, which are a route of a kind, because a quay is where the sea joins the network. The density is low, three routes on nine squares, but each one earns its place: the road reaches every settlement, the promenade links the resort's two halves, and the harbour connects the town to the sea. A network answer on Paper 2 names the types from the key, counts the density, and then does the thinking the counting prepares, which is why the relief explains the detour, the sea explains the harbour, and the resort explains the promenade.
